sentences.zh: 夫恢恢乾德，萬類之所資始；

translations.literal: As for the vast virtue of Qian (Heaven), it is that whereby the myriad kinds receive their beginning;
translations.idiomatic: Heaven's far-reaching creative power is what gives every living kind its first beginning.

sentences.zh: 蕩蕩坤儀，九區之所均載。

translations.literal: The capacious pattern of Kun (Earth) is that on which the nine regions are all borne together.
translations.idiomatic: Earth's encompassing order holds the nine regions on an even plane.

sentences.zh: 考羲軒於往統，肇承天而理物；

translations.literal: Examining Fuxi and the Yellow Emperor in former successions, they began inheriting Heaven and ordering the myriad things;
translations.idiomatic: Tracing Fuxi and the Yellow Emperor through antiquity, the sages first took Heaven's mandate and set the world in order.

sentences.zh: 訊炎昊於前辟，爰制地而疏疆。

translations.literal: Inquiring of Yanhao among former rulers, then they regulated the land and opened up boundaries.
translations.idiomatic: They consulted the luminous forebears, then surveyed the soil and drew its outer marches.

sentences.zh: 襲冠帶以辨諸華，限要荒以殊遐裔，區分中外，其來尚矣。

translations.literal: They inherited caps and sashes to distinguish the Hua (civilized), set bounds at yao and huang to separate the distant margins, and divided inner from outer; from of old this has been esteemed.
translations.idiomatic: Robes and caps marked Chinese civilization, the inner and outer marches fenced off the far hinterlands, and the distinction between the heartland and beyond has been honored since high antiquity.

sentences.zh: 九夷八狄，被青野而亙玄方；

translations.literal: The nine Yi and eight Di spread across the green wilds and span the dark north;
translations.idiomatic: The nine eastern Yi and eight northern Di stretch from green eastern wastes across the somber north.

sentences.zh: 七戎六蠻，綿西宇而橫南極。

translations.literal: The seven Rong and six Man extend through the western realm and stretch across the southern limit.
translations.idiomatic: The seven Rong and six Man peoples thread the western wastes and reach toward the southern edge.

sentences.zh: 繁種落，異君長，遇有道則時遵聲教，鐘無妄則爭肆虔劉，趨扇風塵，蓋其常性也。

translations.literal: They multiply tribes and differ in chieftains; when they encounter a way of virtue they then for a time follow the transforming teachings; when they meet with ill-omened disaster they contend in wanton slaughter; they rush to raise dust in the wind: such is their constant nature.
translations.idiomatic: Tribes proliferate under many chiefs: when the court embodies the Way they heed civilization for a season, but when calamity strikes they turn to raiding; raising turmoil in the borderlands is almost their default bent.

sentences.zh: 詳求遐議，曆選深謨，莫不待以羈縻，防其猾夏。

translations.literal: Carefully seeking far counsel, passing through and selecting deep stratagems, none fail to treat them with loose reins while guarding against their insolence toward the Hua.
translations.idiomatic: Statesmen have long weighed distant counsel and layered plans: the usual answer is loose overlordship on the frontier, backed by vigilance against aggression toward China.

sentences.zh: 武帝受終衰魏，廓境全吳，威略既申，招攜斯廣，迷亂華之議，矜來遠之名，撫舊懷新，歲時無怠，凡四夷入貢者，有二十三國。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu received the mandate in the decline of Wei, broadened the realm and completed Wu; once his might and strategy were displayed, those he summoned and won grew wide; setting aside counsels that would confuse the Hua, he prized the reputation of drawing the far, soothing the old and cherishing the new, yearly without slack; in all, among the four directions' peoples entering tribute there were twenty-three states.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu of Jin succeeded the tottering Wei, swallowed Wu, and let his armies speak, he reached far for allies, brushed aside nativist panic, and burnished the fame of welcoming distant peoples—soothing old clients and courting new ones year after year—until twenty-three foreign realms were sending tribute.

sentences.zh: 既而惠皇失德，中宗遷播，凶徒分據，天邑傾淪，朝化所覃，江外而已，賝貢之禮，於茲殆絕，殊風異俗，所未能詳。

translations.literal: Afterwards Emperor Hui lost virtue, Emperor Zhongzong was driven to wander; fierce bandits partitioned the land, the heavenly capital toppled; where court transforming influence reached was only beyond the Yangzi; the ritual of tribute-gifts here all but ceased; distinctive customs of other lands could not be detailed.
translations.idiomatic: Then the feckless Hui Emperor squandered moral authority, Emperor Yuan fled south, rebels carved up the north, and the capital fell; imperial influence ran only to the lands beyond the river, tribute from abroad nearly stopped, and the finer points of every foreign custom were lost to record.

sentences.zh: 故采其可知者，爲之傳云。

translations.literal: Therefore gathering what can be known, one makes this account for them.
translations.idiomatic: What follows is drawn only from what the sources still allow us to know.

sentences.zh: 北狄竊號中壤，備於載記；

translations.literal: The northern Di usurping titles in the central soil is fully recorded in the annals;
translations.idiomatic: The northern peoples' brief seizure of the heartland is already laid out in the standard histories.

sentences.zh: 在其諸部種類，今略書之。

translations.literal: As for their various branch tribes and kinds, now they are briefly written down.
translations.idiomatic: Their subsidiary tribes are summarized here in outline.

sentences.zh: 東夷

translations.literal: Eastern Yi.
translations.idiomatic: The Eastern Yi.

sentences.zh: 東夷，夫餘國、馬韓、辰韓、肅慎氏、倭人、裨離等十國。

translations.literal: Among the Eastern Yi—Puyŏ, Mahan, Chinhan, the Sushen people, the Wa, Pilü, and others—ten states.
translations.idiomatic: The Eastern Yi section comprises ten polities: Puyŏ, Mahan, Chinhan, the Sushen, the Wa, Pilü, and several others named in the text.

sentences.zh: 夫餘國

translations.literal: The State of Puyŏ.
translations.idiomatic: Puyŏ

sentences.zh: =夫餘國，在玄菟北千餘-{里}-，南接鮮卑，北有弱水，地方二千里，戶八萬，有城邑宮室，地宜五穀。

translations.literal: [Table entry:] Puyŏ lies more than a thousand li north of Xuantu, borders Xianbei to the south, has the Weak Water to the north, its territory is two thousand li square, eighty thousand households, has walled towns, palaces, and houses, and the land suits the five grains.
translations.idiomatic: Puyŏ sits more than a thousand li north of Xuantu Commandery, with Xianbei along its southern frontier and the Weak River to the north; the kingdom spans two thousand square li, counts eighty thousand households, maintains walled towns and palace compounds, and its fields suit the staple grains.

sentences.zh: 其人強勇，會同揖讓之儀有似中國。

translations.literal: Its people are strong and brave; in assemblies and yielding ritual they resemble China.
translations.idiomatic: The people are hardy and bold, and their formal gatherings—with bows and yielding precedence—look much like Chinese court etiquette.

sentences.zh: 其出使，乃衣錦罽，以金銀飾腰。

translations.literal: When they go out on missions, then they wear brocade felt and ornament the waist with gold and silver.
translations.idiomatic: Envoys dress in brocade felts and belt themselves with gold and silver when they travel abroad.

sentences.zh: 其法，殺人者死，沒入其家；

translations.literal: In their laws, one who kills a man dies, and his household is confiscated;
translations.idiomatic: Murder is a capital crime, and the killer's entire household is forfeited to the state.

sentences.zh: 盜者一責十二；

translations.literal: for a thief one pays twelvefold;
translations.idiomatic: Theft is punished with a twelvefold restitution.

sentences.zh: 男女淫，婦人妒，皆殺之。

translations.literal: if men and women commit lewdness, or a wife is jealous, all are killed.
translations.idiomatic: Adultery and wifely jealousy alike carry the death penalty.

sentences.zh: 若有軍事，殺牛祭天，以其蹄占吉凶，蹄解者爲凶，合者爲吉。

translations.literal: If there is military business, they slaughter an ox and sacrifice to Heaven, and by its hooves divine auspicious or inauspicious; if the hooves split apart it is inauspicious, if they stay joined it is auspicious.
translations.idiomatic: Before a campaign they sacrifice an ox to Heaven and read the hooves: split hooves mean ill luck, closed hooves mean a good omen.

sentences.zh: 死者以生人殉葬，有槨無棺。

translations.literal: For the dead they bury living persons with them; they have an outer coffin but no inner coffin.
translations.idiomatic: The dead take human victims into the grave; burials use an outer shell but no inner coffin.

sentences.zh: 其居喪，男女皆衣純白，婦人著布面衣，去玉佩。

translations.literal: In their mourning, men and women all wear pure white; women put on cloth face-veils and remove jade pendants.
translations.idiomatic: Mourners of both sexes dress entirely in white; women veil their faces in plain cloth and lay aside their jade ornaments.

sentences.zh: 出善馬及貂豽、美珠，珠大如酸棗。

translations.literal: They produce fine horses, sable and wildcat pelts, and beautiful pearls; the pearls are as large as sour jujubes.
translations.idiomatic: Their exports include fine horses, sable and wildcat furs, and lustrous pearls the size of small jujubes.

sentences.zh: 其國殷富，自先世以來，未嘗被破。

translations.literal: Their state is prosperous; from former generations onward it has never been broken.
translations.idiomatic: The realm is wealthy, and for generations it had never been conquered—until later troubles.

sentences.zh: 其王印文稱「穢王之印」。

translations.literal: The inscription on their king's seal reads 'Seal of the King of Mo' (the text uses the graph commonly read hui for this ethnonym).
translations.idiomatic: The royal seal bears the legend 'Seal of the King of Mo,' reflecting the older graph still carved on Puyŏ regalia.

sentences.zh: 國中有古穢城，本穢貃之城也。

translations.literal: Within the state there is an ancient Mo city; originally it was a city of the Mo Mo (Huimo) people.
translations.idiomatic: The kingdom still holds an old fortress called Mo City, traditionally the seat of the Huimo (Hui-Mo) confederation.

sentences.zh: 武帝時，頻來朝貢，至，爲慕容廆所襲破，其王依慮自殺，子弟走保沃沮。

translations.literal: In Emperor Wu's time they came frequently to court tribute; when they arrived, Murong Hui attacked and broke them; their king Yilü killed himself, and sons and younger kin fled to defend themselves in Okjeo.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Wu they often sent tribute, but on one such mission Murong Hui shattered their host; King Yilü took his own life, while princes and kinsmen fled into the Okjeo marshes for safety.

sentences.zh: 帝爲下詔曰：「夫餘王世守忠孝，爲惡虜所滅，其湣念之。

translations.literal: The emperor therefore issued an edict saying: 'The kings of Puyŏ have generation after generation kept faith and filial piety; they were destroyed by evil invaders—We pity and think on them.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor issued an edict: 'Puyŏ's kings have long upheld loyalty and filial duty; a vicious foe wiped them out, and the court grieves for them.'

sentences.zh: 若其遺類足以復國者，當爲之方計，使得存立。

translations.literal: If among their surviving kind there are those sufficient to restore the state, We ought to devise a plan for them, enabling them to survive and stand.'
translations.idiomatic: If enough survivors remain to rebuild the kingdom, ministers should lay plans so the state can endure.'

sentences.zh: 」有司奏護東夷校尉鮮于嬰不救夫餘，失於機略。

translations.literal: ' The responsible offices memorialized that the Protecting Colonel of the Eastern Yi, Xianyu Ying, had not rescued Puyŏ and had failed in timely strategy.
translations.idiomatic: ' The bureaus reported that Xianyu Ying, Colonel of the Eastern Yi, had withheld relief from Puyŏ and mishandled the crisis.

sentences.zh: 詔免嬰，以何龕代之。

translations.literal: An edict dismissed Ying and replaced him with He Kan.
translations.idiomatic: An edict removed Ying from office and appointed He Kan in his place.

sentences.zh: 明年，夫餘後王依羅遣詣龕，求率見人還復舊國。

translations.literal: The next year the later king of Puyŏ, Yiluo, sent someone to Kan, seeking to lead the remnant people back and restore the old state.
translations.idiomatic: The following year King Yiluo of the restored line appealed to He Kan, asking to lead his people home and refound the kingdom.

sentences.zh: 仍請援。

translations.literal: He also requested aid.
translations.idiomatic: He also begged for military support.

sentences.zh: 龕上列，遣督郵賈沈以兵送之。

translations.literal: Kan submitted the particulars and dispatched the surveillance officer Jia Shen with troops to escort them.
translations.idiomatic: He Kan forwarded the petition and sent the inspector Jia Shen with an escort to convoy them north.

sentences.zh: 廆又要之于路，沈與戰，大敗之，廆衆退，羅得復國。

translations.literal: Hui again waylaid them on the road; Shen fought him, greatly defeated him, Hui's host withdrew, and Yiluo was able to restore the state.
translations.idiomatic: Murong Hui tried to ambush the column; Jia Shen gave battle, routed him decisively, and Yiluo recovered his kingdom once the Murong forces pulled back.

sentences.zh: 爾後每爲廆掠其種人，賣於中國。

translations.literal: Afterwards repeatedly Hui plundered their tribesmen and sold them in China.
translations.idiomatic: Thereafter Murong Hui repeatedly raided Puyŏ captives and sold them into the Central Plains slave markets.

sentences.zh: 帝湣之，又發詔以官物贖還，下司、冀二州，禁市夫餘之口。

translations.literal: The emperor pitied them, again issued an edict to ransom them back with government goods, and ordered the two provinces Si and Ji to forbid marketing Puyŏ persons.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor took pity, ordered officials to buy the captives back with state funds, and instructed Si and Ji provinces to ban the sale of Puyŏ people.

sentences.zh: 三韓

translations.literal: The Three Han.
translations.idiomatic: The Three Han (Samhan)

translations.literal: The line is an equals sign used as a table marker in the transmitted layout.
translations.idiomatic: — (source table divider)

sentences.zh: 韓種有三：一曰馬韓，二曰辰韓，三曰弁韓。

translations.literal: The Han kinds are three: first called Mahan, second called Chinhan, third called Pyŏnhan.
translations.idiomatic: The Han peoples fall into three branches: Mahan, Chinhan, and Pyŏnhan (Byŏnhan).

sentences.zh: 辰韓在帶方南，東西以海爲限。

translations.literal: Chinhan is south of Daifang, east and west bounded by the sea.
translations.idiomatic: Chinhan lies south of Daifang Commandery, hemmed by ocean on both east and west.

sentences.zh: 馬韓居山海之間，無城郭，凡有小國五十六所，大者萬戶，小者數千家，各有渠帥。

translations.literal: Mahan dwells between mountains and sea, without walls and moats; in all there are fifty-six small states, large ones ten thousand households, small ones several thousand households, each having its chieftain.
translations.idiomatic: Mahan occupies the belt between coast and hills without walled cities: fifty-six petty chiefdoms, the largest near ten thousand households, the smallest a few thousand, each under its own headman.

sentences.zh: 俗少綱紀，無跪拜之禮。

translations.literal: Their customs lack much order; they have no ritual of kneeling and bowing.
translations.idiomatic: Customs are loosely ordered, and they observe no formal kneeling-and-bowing etiquette.

sentences.zh: 居處作土室，形如塚，其戶向上，舉家共在其中，無長幼男女之別。

translations.literal: Their dwellings are earthen chambers shaped like tombs; the door faces upward; the whole household shares the inside together, without distinction of old and young, male and female.
translations.idiomatic: They live in tomb-shaped earthen huts with roof hatches; entire families crowd inside without separating elders from youths or men from women.

sentences.zh: 不知乘牛馬，畜者但以送葬。

translations.literal: They do not know how to ride oxen and horses; those they keep they use only to send off burials.
translations.idiomatic: They neither ride cattle nor horses; livestock is kept solely for funeral processions.

sentences.zh: 俗不重金銀錦罽，而貴瓔珠，用以綴衣或飾發垂耳。

translations.literal: Their customs do not esteem gold, silver, or brocade felts, but prize strung pearls, using them to trim garments or adorn the hair hanging at the ears.
translations.idiomatic: Gold, silver, and brocade matter little; strings of pearls are treasured for trimming robes or dangling from hair and ears.

sentences.zh: 其男子科頭露紒，衣布袍，履草蹻，性勇悍。

translations.literal: Their men shave the crown and expose the topknot, wear cloth robes, tread straw sandals, and by nature are fierce and hardy.
translations.idiomatic: Men shave their crowns, knot their hair atop bare scalps, wear plain gowns and straw sandals, and are fierce by temperament.

sentences.zh: 國中有所調役，及起築城隍，年少勇健者皆鑿其背皮，貫以大繩，以杖搖繩，終日歡呼力作，不以爲痛。

translations.literal: Whenever in the state there are levied corvée duties, or raising and building city walls and moats, the young who are brave and strong all bore the skin of their backs, thread great ropes through, and with staffs shake the ropes, shouting joyfully in labor all day, not thinking it painful.
translations.idiomatic: When corvée gangs go out to raise city walls, the young and hardy have ropes threaded through slits cut in their backs; foremen swing the lines with poles while the workers whoop through the day as if they felt no pain.

sentences.zh: 善用弓楯矛櫓，雖有鬥爭攻戰，而貴相屈服。

translations.literal: They are skilled with bow, shield, spear, and great shield; although there are quarrels, attacks, and battles, they esteem yielding to one another.
translations.idiomatic: They handle bows, shields, spears, and pavises well; even in battle they prize forcing the foe to submit rather than annihilating him.

sentences.zh: 俗信鬼神，常以五月耕種畢，群聚歌舞以祭神；

translations.literal: Their customs trust ghosts and spirits; they constantly in the fifth month, when plowing and planting are finished, gather in crowds to sing and dance in order to sacrifice to the spirits;
translations.idiomatic: They are spirit-fearing: each fifth month, after the spring planting ends, whole villages gather to sing, dance, and sacrifice.

sentences.zh: 至十月農事畢，亦如之。

translations.literal: when it reaches the tenth month and farm work is finished, it is likewise.
translations.idiomatic: They repeat the festival in the tenth month when the harvest work is done.

sentences.zh: 國邑各立一人主祭天神，謂爲天君。

translations.literal: Each state and town establishes one man to preside at sacrifice to the celestial spirit, called the Lord of Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: Every chiefdom appoints a single priest of the sky god, locally titled 'Lord of Heaven.'

sentences.zh: 又置別邑，名曰蘇塗，立大木，懸鈴鼓。

translations.literal: They also set up separate settlements called Sutu, erect great trees, and hang bells and drums.
translations.idiomatic: They maintain sacred precincts called Sutu, where tall poles carry bells and drums for ritual.

sentences.zh: 其蘇塗之義，有似西域浮屠也，而所行善惡有異。

translations.literal: As for the meaning of these Sutu, they are somewhat like the Western Regions' Buddha, yet in what they practice of good and evil there are differences.
translations.idiomatic: The Sutu cult resembles the Buddhist shrines of the Western Regions in outward form, though its moral teaching diverges sharply.

sentences.zh: 武帝、二年，其主頻遣使入貢方物，七年、八年、十年，又頻至。

translations.literal: In Emperor Wu's reign, the second year, their ruler repeatedly dispatched envoys to enter tribute of local products; in the seventh, eighth, and tenth years they again came frequently.
translations.idiomatic: In the second year of Emperor Wu's reign their chief kept sending envoys with local tribute, and he appeared again often in the seventh, eighth, and tenth years.

sentences.zh: ，詣東夷校尉何龕上獻。

translations.literal: (Continuing the account,) they proceeded to the Colonel of the Eastern Yi, He Kan, to present the tribute upward.
translations.idiomatic: They then went to He Kan, Colonel of the Eastern Yi, to deliver the presentation.

sentences.zh: 復來，明年又請內附。

translations.literal: They came again; the next year again they requested to attach inward.
translations.idiomatic: They returned the next season, and the year after that petitioned to be enrolled as imperial subjects.

sentences.zh: 辰韓在馬韓之東，自言秦之亡人避役入韓，韓割東界以居之，立城柵，言語有類秦人，由是或謂之爲秦韓。

translations.literal: Chinhan is east of Mahan; they themselves say they are Qin fugitives who fled corvée and entered Han; Han ceded the eastern border to house them, set up stockades, and their speech resembles Qin people; hence some call them Qin Han.
translations.idiomatic: Chinhan lies east of Mahan; by their own account they are Qin dynasty runaways who crossed the border to escape labor levies, were given the eastern marches to settle, built palisaded towns, and speak a dialect close to old Qin speech—so outsiders sometimes call them 'Qin Han.'

sentences.zh: 初有六國，後稍分爲十二，又有弁辰，亦十二國，合四五萬戶，各有渠帥，皆屬於辰韓。

translations.literal: At first there were six states, afterwards gradually they divided into twelve; further there is Pyŏnjin, also twelve states, together forty or fifty thousand households, each having its chieftain, and all belong to Chinhan.
translations.idiomatic: They began as six chiefdoms that later split into twelve; Pyŏnjin adds another dozen polities, altogether some forty or fifty thousand households under local headmen, all owing allegiance to Chinhan.

sentences.zh: 辰韓常用馬韓人作主，雖世世相承，而不得自立，明其流移之人，故爲馬韓所制也。

translations.literal: Chinhan constantly uses Mahan people to act as rulers; although generation after generation they succeed one another, they cannot establish themselves independently, which clarifies that they are transplanted people, therefore are controlled by Mahan.
translations.idiomatic: Chinhan routinely installs Mahan nobles as puppet kings; succession continues, yet native rulers never gain real independence—clear proof that these are immigrant lineages held in check by Mahan.

sentences.zh: 地宜五穀，俗饒蠶桑，善作縑布，服牛乘馬。

translations.literal: The land suits the five grains; their customs are rich in silkworms and mulberry; they are skilled at making plain cloth; they yoke oxen and ride horses.
translations.idiomatic: The soil supports the staple grains, sericulture thrives, homespun is excellent, and the people both plow with oxen and ride horses.

sentences.zh: 其風俗可類馬韓，兵器亦與之同。

translations.literal: Their customs can be classed with Mahan; weapons likewise are the same as theirs.
translations.idiomatic: Daily life resembles Mahan, and their arms match Mahan patterns.

sentences.zh: 初生子，便以石押其頭使扁。

translations.literal: When a child is first born, then with a stone they press its head to make it flat.
translations.idiomatic: Newborns have a stone pressed on the skull to flatten the forehead—a deliberate ideal of beauty.

sentences.zh: 喜舞，善彈瑟，瑟形似築。

translations.literal: They delight in dance and are skilled at plucking the se; the se's shape resembles the zhu.
translations.idiomatic: They love dancing and play the se zither well; the instrument looks like a hammered zhu.

sentences.zh: 武帝，其王遣使獻方物。

translations.literal: Emperor Wu— their king dispatched envoys to present local products.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Wu their ruler sent envoys bearing regional tribute.

sentences.zh: 二年復來朝貢，七年又來。

translations.literal: The second year they again came to court tribute; the seventh year they again came.
translations.idiomatic: They returned for court audience in the second year and again in the seventh.

sentences.zh: 肅慎氏

translations.literal: The Sushen people.
translations.idiomatic: Sushen

sentences.zh: =肅慎氏一名挹婁，在不咸山北，去夫餘可六十日行。

translations.literal: [Table entry:] The Sushen people, also called Yilou, are north of Mount Buxian, distant from Puyŏ by roughly sixty days' travel.
translations.idiomatic: The Sushen—also known as Yilou—live north of Mount Buxian, about sixty days' march from Puyŏ.

sentences.zh: 東濱大海，西接寇漫汗國，北極弱水。

translations.literal: East they border the great sea; west they adjoin the state of Koumanhan; north they reach the Weak Water.
translations.idiomatic: They front the sea on the east, touch the Koumanhan polity on the west, and run northward to the Weak River.

sentences.zh: 其土界廣袤數千里，居深山窮谷，其路險阻，車馬不通。

translations.literal: Their territory's bounds extend several thousand li; they dwell in deep mountains and exhausted valleys; their roads are perilous and blocked; carts and horses do not pass.
translations.idiomatic: Their domain spans thousands of li of rugged highlands; paths are so treacherous that carts and horses cannot penetrate.

sentences.zh: 夏則巢居，冬則穴處。

translations.literal: In summer they nest-dwell; in winter they cave-dwell.
translations.idiomatic: Summer homes are platforms in the trees; winter shelter is dug into the earth.

sentences.zh: 父子世爲君長。

translations.literal: Fathers and sons generation after generation act as lords and chiefs.
translations.idiomatic: Chieftainship passes from father to son without break.

sentences.zh: 無文墨，以言語爲約。

translations.literal: They have no writing or ink; they take spoken words as covenants.
translations.idiomatic: They keep no written records; agreements are sealed by word of mouth alone.

sentences.zh: 有馬不乘，但以爲財產而已。

translations.literal: They have horses but do not ride them; they only take them as property goods.
translations.idiomatic: Horses are hoarded as wealth, not ridden for transport.

sentences.zh: 無牛羊，多畜豬，食其肉，衣其皮，績毛以爲布。

translations.literal: They lack oxen and sheep; they raise many pigs, eat their flesh, wear their skins, and spin hair to make cloth.
translations.idiomatic: Cattle and sheep are absent, but pig herds are large; they eat pork, wear pigskin, and weave animal hair into cloth.

sentences.zh: 有樹名雒常，若中國有聖帝代立，則其木生皮可衣。

translations.literal: There is a tree called Luochang; if in China there is a sage emperor who replaces the throne, then that tree produces bark that can be worn as clothing.
translations.idiomatic: They revere a 'Luochang' tree whose bark, they say, becomes wearable whenever a sage Son of Heaven ascends in China.

sentences.zh: 無井灶，作瓦鬲，受四五升以食。

translations.literal: They have no wells or stoves; they make pottery li that hold four or five sheng for eating.
translations.idiomatic: They cook without proper hearths or wells, using small earthen cauldrons that hold only a few pints of food.

sentences.zh: 坐則箕踞，以足挾肉而啖之，得凍肉，坐其上令暖。

translations.literal: When sitting they sit with legs spread; they clamp meat with the feet and eat it; when they obtain frozen meat, they sit on it to make it warm.
translations.idiomatic: They squat with knees wide, pinch meat between the toes to eat, and thaw frozen cuts by sitting on them.

sentences.zh: 土無鹽鐵，燒木作灰，灌取汁而食之。

translations.literal: Their soil lacks salt and iron; they burn wood to make ash, pour water to extract juice, and eat it.
translations.idiomatic: With no native salt or iron, they leach lye from wood ash and drink the bitter brine.

sentences.zh: 俗皆編發，以布作襜，徑尺餘，以蔽前後。

translations.literal: Their custom is all to braid the hair; they make aprons of cloth more than a chi in diameter to cover front and back.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone braids the hair and wraps the body in a foot-wide cloth apron front and back.

sentences.zh: 將嫁娶，男以毛羽插女頭，女和則持歸，然後致禮娉之。

translations.literal: When about to marry, the man inserts feathers in the woman's head; if the woman is pleased then he carries her home, afterwards presenting the rites and betrothing her.
translations.idiomatic: Courtship begins when a suitor sticks plumes in a girl's hair; if she accepts, he carries her home and only then completes bride-price formalities.

sentences.zh: 婦貞而女淫，貴壯而賤老，死者其日即葬之於野，交木作小槨，殺豬積其上，以爲死者之糧。

translations.literal: Wives are chaste but girls are promiscuous; they esteem the strong and despise the old; on the day a person dies they immediately bury him in the wild, cross timbers to make a small outer coffin, slaughter pigs and pile them on top, taking them as provisions for the dead.
translations.idiomatic: Married women are expected to be faithful while maidens may take lovers; the strong are honored and the aged slighted; corpses go to the field the same day under a lattice of logs, with slaughtered pigs stacked above as provisions for the ghost.

sentences.zh: 性凶悍，以無憂哀相尚。

translations.literal: By nature they are fierce and hardy; they esteem having no grief or sorrow.
translations.idiomatic: They are truculent by nature and admire a show of dry-eyed stoicism.

sentences.zh: 父母死，男子不哭泣，哭者謂之不壯。

translations.literal: When father and mother die, men do not weep; one who weeps is called not stalwart.
translations.idiomatic: Sons must not cry at a parent's funeral—tears are read as weakness.

sentences.zh: 相盜竊，無多少皆殺之，故雖野處而不相犯。

translations.literal: If they steal from one another, without regard to much or little all are killed; therefore although they dwell in the wilds they do not violate one another.
translations.idiomatic: Theft of any amount is punished with death, which keeps even scattered hamlets from robbing neighbors.

sentences.zh: 有石砮，皮骨之甲，檀弓三尺五寸，楛矢長尺有咫。

translations.literal: They have stone arrowheads, armor of hide and bone, sandalwood bows three chi five cun long, and oak arrows a chi and eight cun long.
translations.idiomatic: Their kit includes stone arrowheads, hide-and-bone armor, sandalwood bows three and a half feet long, and oak-shafted arrows eighteen inches in length.

sentences.zh: 其國東北有山出石，其利入鐵，將取之，必先祈神。

translations.literal: In the state's northeast there is a mountain that produces stone; its sharpness enters iron; when they are about to take it, they must first pray to the spirits.
translations.idiomatic: A northeastern peak yields a stone as hard as cast iron; miners pray to the spirits before they cut any out.

sentences.zh: 周武王時，獻其楛矢、石砮。

translations.literal: In King Wu of Zhou's time they presented their oak arrows and stone arrowheads.
translations.idiomatic: In the days of King Wu of Zhou they already offered tribute of oak-shafted arrows and stone heads.

sentences.zh: 逮于周公輔成王，復遣使入賀，爾後千餘年，雖秦漢之盛，莫之致也。

translations.literal: Reaching to the Duke of Zhou assisting King Cheng, they again dispatched envoys to enter congratulations; afterwards more than a thousand years, although Qin and Han were flourishing, none could bring them in.
translations.idiomatic: They sent another mission when the Duke of Zhou ruled for the boy king Cheng, then fell silent for a millennium—even the might of Qin and Han could not draw them back to court.

sentences.zh: 及文帝作相，魏景元末，來貢楛矢、石砮、弓甲、貂皮之屬。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wen served as chancellor, at the end of Wei Jingyuan, they came to tribute oak arrows, stone arrowheads, bow armor, sable pelts, and the like.
translations.idiomatic: Late in Wei's Jingyuan era, while Sima Yan still held the chancellorship, they renewed contact with gifts of arrows, stone heads, armor, and sable skins.

sentences.zh: 魏帝詔歸於相府，賜其王傉雞錦罽、綿帛。

translations.literal: The Wei emperor ordered the goods returned to the chancellor's office and bestowed on their king Nuji brocade felts and silks.
translations.idiomatic: The Wei court forwarded the tribute to the chancellor's bureau and sent King Nuji brocades and silks in return.

sentences.zh: 至武帝元康初，復來貢獻。

translations.literal: Reaching Emperor Wu's Yuankang beginning, they again came with tribute offerings.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Emperor Wu's Yuankang reign they appeared at court once more.

sentences.zh: 元帝中興，又詣江左貢其石砮。

translations.literal: When Emperor Yuan restored the dynasty, they again went to the left of the Yangzi to tribute their stone arrowheads.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Yuan revived the house south of the river, they crossed the Yangzi to present another gift of stone arrowheads.

sentences.zh: 至成帝時，通貢于石季龍，四年方達。

translations.literal: Reaching Emperor Cheng's time, they opened communication of tribute to Shi Jilong; only after four years did it arrive.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Cheng they sent tribute toward Shi Hu, but the mission needed four years to complete the journey.

sentences.zh: 季龍問之，答曰：「每候牛馬向西南眠者三年矣，是知有大國所在，故來一云。」

translations.literal: Jilong asked them; they answered saying: 'We have watched for three years how oxen and horses lie down with heads toward the southwest; by this we knew there was a great state located there, therefore we came once to declare it.'
translations.idiomatic: Shi Hu questioned the envoys, who replied: 'For three years our herds have slept facing southwest—an omen that a great realm lies in that direction—so we came to seek it.'

sentences.zh: 倭人

translations.literal: The Wa people.
translations.idiomatic: The Wa (Japan)

sentences.zh: =在帶方東南大海中，依山島為國。

translations.literal: [Table entry:] They are in the great sea southeast of Daifang, relying on mountains and islands to form their state.
translations.idiomatic: They dwell in the ocean southeast of Daifang Commandery, building their kingdom on clustered islands and coastal hills.

sentences.zh: 地多山林，無良田，食海物。

translations.literal: The land has many mountains and forests, lacks good fields, and they eat sea creatures.
translations.idiomatic: Forested hills dominate and arable soil is scarce, so the diet relies heavily on seafood.

sentences.zh: 舊有百餘小國相接，至魏時，有三十國通好，戶有七萬。

translations.literal: Formerly there were more than a hundred small states adjoining one another; reaching Wei times, thirty states had opened friendship, and households numbered seventy thousand.
translations.idiomatic: Legend speaks of over a hundred petty realms; by the Wei period thirty still exchanged embassies, with some seventy thousand households all told.

sentences.zh: 男子無大小，悉黥面文身，自謂太伯之後。

translations.literal: Men, without regard to age, all tattoo the face and pattern the body, calling themselves posterity of Taibo.
translations.idiomatic: Every male, young or old, tattoos face and limbs and claims descent from Taibo of Wu.

sentences.zh: 又言上古使詣中國，皆自稱大夫。

translations.literal: They further say that in high antiquity when envoys went to China, all styled themselves grandees.
translations.idiomatic: They add that ancient envoys to the Central Plains always presented themselves with the Chinese title 'grandee.'

sentences.zh: 昔夏少康之子封於會稽，斷髮文身以避蛟龍之害。

translations.literal: Formerly Shaokang of Xia's son was enfeoffed at Kuaiji; he cut the hair and patterned the body to avoid harm from horned dragons.
translations.idiomatic: They cite the son of Xia Shaokang, enfeoffed at Kuaiji, who cropped his hair and tattooed his skin to ward off river dragons.

sentences.zh: 今倭人好沈沒取魚，亦文身以厭水禽。

translations.literal: Now the Wa people delight in diving to seize fish, and likewise pattern the body to repel water birds.
translations.idiomatic: Today's Wa are avid pearl divers and fishermen, tattooing themselves, they say, to frighten away sharks and sea monsters.

sentences.zh: 計其道里，當會稽東冶之東。

translations.literal: Calculating their route distance, they ought to be east of Kuaiji's eastern Ye.
translations.idiomatic: By dead reckoning their archipelago lies east of the Eastern Ye naval station in old Kuaiji.

sentences.zh: 其男子衣以橫幅，但結束相連，略無縫綴。

translations.literal: Their men clothe themselves with horizontal cloth strips, only tying and binding them linked together, with almost no stitching.
translations.idiomatic: Men wrap themselves in a single bolt of cloth, belted into place with almost no needlework.

sentences.zh: 婦人衣如單被，穿其中央以貫頭，而皆被髮徒跣。

translations.literal: Women's garments are like a single coverlet; they pierce the center to pass the head through, and all let hair hang loose and go barefoot.
translations.idiomatic: Women wear poncho-like shifts with a head hole cut in the middle, hair unbound and feet bare.

sentences.zh: 其地溫暖，俗種禾稻紵麻而蠶桑織績。

translations.literal: Their land is warm; by custom they plant grain, rice, ramie, and hemp, and raise silkworms and mulberry for weaving and spinning.
translations.idiomatic: The climate is mild; they grow rice, hemp, and ramie, and practice sericulture for cloth.

sentences.zh: 土無牛馬，有刀楯弓箭，以鐵為鏃。

translations.literal: Their soil lacks oxen and horses; they have knives, shields, bows, and arrows, and use iron for arrowheads.
translations.idiomatic: Cattle and horses are absent, but iron-tipped bows, knives, and shields are common.

sentences.zh: 有屋宇，父母兄弟臥息異處。

translations.literal: They have roofed houses; fathers, mothers, brothers sleep and rest in separate places.
translations.idiomatic: They build proper houses, yet fathers, mothers, and brothers sleep in separate rooms.

sentences.zh: 食飲用俎豆。

translations.literal: For eating and drinking they use stands and bowls.
translations.idiomatic: Meals are served on Chinese-style stands and trenchers.

sentences.zh: 嫁娶不持錢帛，以衣迎之。

translations.literal: In marrying they do not bring cash or silks; with garments they welcome the bride.
translations.idiomatic: Marriages need no bride-price in coin; a gift of robes suffices to fetch the bride.

sentences.zh: 死有棺無槨，封土為冢。

translations.literal: For death they have inner coffins but no outer coffin; they mound earth to make a tomb.
translations.idiomatic: Burials use inner coffins only, heaped over with a simple earthen mound.

sentences.zh: 初喪，哭泣不食肉，已葬，舉家入水澡浴自潔，以除不祥。

translations.literal: At first mourning they weep and do not eat meat; after burial, the whole household enters water to bathe and cleanse themselves, thereby removing ill-omen.
translations.idiomatic: Mourners wail and abstain from meat until the funeral; afterward the entire family bathes in a stream to wash away pollution.

sentences.zh: 其舉大事，輒灼骨以占吉凶。

translations.literal: Whenever they undertake great affairs, then they scorch bone to divine auspicious or inauspicious.
translations.idiomatic: Major decisions are preceded by scapulimancy—cracking heated bones for omens.

sentences.zh: 不知正歲四節，但計秋收之時以為年紀。

translations.literal: They do not know correct new year or the four seasons; they only reckon by the time of autumn harvest to make the year count.
translations.idiomatic: They ignore the Chinese calendar; a year is reckoned from harvest to harvest.

sentences.zh: 人多壽百年，或八九十。

translations.literal: People mostly live to a hundred years, or eighty or ninety.
translations.idiomatic: Many live a full century; octogenarians are common.

sentences.zh: 國多婦女，不淫不妒。

translations.literal: The state has many women; they are not promiscuous and not jealous.
translations.idiomatic: Women outnumber men, yet adultery and jealousy are rare.

sentences.zh: 無爭訟。

translations.literal: There are no quarrels or lawsuits.
translations.idiomatic: Litigation is practically unknown.

sentences.zh: 犯輕罪者沒其妻孥，重者族滅其家。

translations.literal: Those who commit light crimes have wives and children confiscated; for heavy ones the clan is exterminated to the household.
translations.idiomatic: Petty crime costs a man his wife and children; serious crime brings extermination of the whole lineage.

sentences.zh: 舊以男子為主，漢末倭人亂，攻伐不定，乃立女子爲王，名曰卑彌呼。

translations.literal: Formerly they used men as rulers; at the end of Han the Wa people were in chaos, attacks and raids unsettled, therefore they established a woman as king, named Himiko.
translations.idiomatic: Kings had always been male, but the late-Han turmoil among the Wa produced endless civil war until the chiefs raised a woman named Himiko to the throne.

sentences.zh: 宣帝之平公孫氏也，其女王遣使至帶方朝見，其後貢聘不絶。

translations.literal: When Emperor Xuan pacified the Gongsun clan, their woman king dispatched envoys to Daifang to court audience; afterwards tribute missions did not cease.
translations.idiomatic: After Sima Yi crushed the Gongsun regime, Queen Himiko sent envoys to Daifang, and tribute thereafter never stopped.

sentences.zh: 及文帝作相，又數至。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wen served as chancellor, they again came several times.
translations.idiomatic: During Sima Zhao's regency they visited repeatedly.

sentences.zh: 泰始初，遣使重譯入貢。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Taishi, they dispatched envoys through double translation to enter tribute.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Taishi era they again sent missions, relayed through interpreters, bearing tribute.

sentences.zh: 裨離

translations.literal: Pilü.
translations.idiomatic: Pilü

sentences.zh: =裨離國在肅慎西北，馬行可二百日，領戶二萬。

translations.literal: [Table entry:] The state of Pilü is northwest of the Sushen; by horse travel it is roughly two hundred days, and it leads twenty thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: Pilü lies northwest of the Sushen country, some two hundred days' ride away, with about twenty thousand households.

sentences.zh: 養雲國去裨離馬行又五十日，領戶二萬。

translations.literal: The state of Yangyun is fifty days' horse travel from Pilü farther on, and leads twenty thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: Yangyun is another fifty days' ride beyond Pilü and also claims twenty thousand households.

sentences.zh: 寇莫汗國去養雲國又百日行，領戶五萬餘。

translations.literal: The state of Kou Mohan is another hundred days' travel from Yangyun, and leads more than fifty thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: Kou Mohan lies a hundred days beyond Yangyun and numbers over fifty thousand households.

sentences.zh: 一群國去莫汗又百五十日，計去肅慎五萬餘-{里}-。

translations.literal: The state of Yiqun is another hundred fifty days from Mohan; calculating from the Sushen it is more than fifty thousand li.
translations.idiomatic: Yiqun is a hundred fifty days past Mohan—well over fifty thousand li from the Sushen heartland by the reckoning here.

sentences.zh: 其風俗土壤並未詳。

translations.literal: Their customs, soil, and patterns are not detailed.
translations.idiomatic: Their manners and terrain are nowhere described in detail.

sentences.zh: ，各遣小部獻其方物。

translations.literal: (Continuing,) each dispatched small detachments to present their local products.
translations.idiomatic: Each of these peoples then sent minor parties with regional tribute.

sentences.zh: 至太熙初，復有牟奴國帥逸芝惟離、模盧國帥沙支臣芝、於離末利國帥加牟臣芝、蒲都國帥因末、繩全國帥馬路、沙樓國帥釤加，各遣正副使詣東夷校尉何龕歸化。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Taixi, there were again the chief of the Mourou state Yizhi Weili, the chief of the Molu state Shazhi Chenzhi, the chief of the Yulimoli state Jiamou Chenzhi, the chief of the Pudu state Yinmo, the chief of the Shengquan state Malu, and the chief of the Shalou state Shan Jia; each dispatched principal and deputy envoys to the Colonel of the Eastern Yi, He Kan, to submit and be transformed.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Taixi era, chiefs named Yizhi Weili of Mourou, Shazhi Chenzhi of Molu, Jiamou Chenzhi of Yulimoli, Yinmo of Pudu, Malu of Shengquan, and Shan Jia of Shalou each sent paired envoys to Colonel He Kan to offer allegiance.

sentences.zh: 西戎

translations.literal: Western Rong.
translations.idiomatic: The Western Rong

sentences.zh: 西戎，吐谷渾、焉耆國、龜茲國、大宛國、康居國、大秦國、吐谷渾、吐延、葉延、辟奚、視連、視羆、樹洛幹。

translations.literal: Among the Western Rong—Tuyuhun, Yanqi, Kucha, Dayuan, Kangju, Da Qin, Tuyuhun, Tuyan, Yeyan, Pixi, Shilian, Shirong, Shuluogan.
translations.idiomatic: The Western Rong chapter lists Tuyuhun (with sub-biographies for Tuyan, Yeyan, Pixi, Shilian, Shirong, and Shuluogan), Yanqi, Kucha, Dayuan, Kangju, and Da Qin.
